public_rationale: OpenAI's January 8 statement defended training on publicly available internet material as fair use. That supports the contextual claim that it wanted to continue using some copyrighted material without obtaining individual paid licences. Its Axel Springer agreement qualifies the rhetoric: OpenAI also pursued publisher partnerships covering training. The evidence supports rejection of an exclusively licensed approach, not rejection of all licensing or proof of every unpaid use.
limitations: The result depends on the contextual reading that Marcus meant an exclusively public-domain or licensed approach.
Public advocacy establishes a corporate position, not private motives.
The sources do not prove that OpenAI's use was unlawful.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI does not want to take approaches as conventional as training only on public domain data or licensing other data, and instead wants to keep using copyrighted materials, apparently without paying for them.

statement.excerpt: But OpenAI doesn’t want to do anything nearly as conventional as that. They want to continue to use copyrighted materials, apparently without paying for them.
statement.document_title: DALL-E’s New Guardrails: Fast, Furious, and Far from Airtight

from_speaker: doesn’t want to do anything nearly as conventional as that
our_interpretation: Read in context, OpenAI was unwilling to restrict all training material to public-domain or individually licensed sources.
The payment allegation concerns at least some copyrighted material, rather than an assertion that OpenAI never paid or licensed anyone.
Assess stated corporate policy through the latest pre-post public statements in January 2024, using January 1–10 as the observation window. Corporate policy has no quarterly reporting period.
Public statements can establish an advocated policy, but cannot directly establish private motives or every payment.
This is a qualitative training-policy claim, not a quantified company spending claim.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous OpenAI statements advocate continued use of copyrighted training material under a legal rationale that does not require individual paid licences.
criteria.contradiction_condition: OpenAI had committed to using exclusively public-domain or appropriately licensed training material and had abandoned reliance on unlicensed copyrighted material.

evidence.explanation: OpenAI publicly defended internet-based training under fair use rather than committing to obtain permission for all material. This establishes its position, not the legal correctness of that position.

This materially qualifies any suggestion that OpenAI rejected publisher agreements altogether. It predates the selected January observation window and does not establish a policy of licensing every training source.
